results.note: "This is not the time for full pruning" is stated flat, but AF-3 records that sources differ (C-1): Ask Extension #615970 says pruning "only becomes a problem if you have a couple of inches of new growth already leafed out". The disagreement and the new-growth limit are not shown (rule 2, rule 10). AF-4 only places major pruning at or near bud break; it says nothing against later pruning. "Can cost you flowers" is stronger than DA-APR ("might delay flowering a little"); OSU says "reduce flowering". "You can still remove" for a rose already in leaf rests on AF-2/AF-17 (Low, with the condition "without damaging the foliage"), not on AF-1 (Moderate, generic "at any time"), so Moderate is too high for that clause and the condition is missing.
results.suggested_wording: Your rose is already growing, so full pruning now is likely to reduce or delay flowering. One source says pruning is fine until there is a couple of inches of new growth. Dead, damaged or diseased wood can still be removed, but go gently so you do not damage the new leaves.

results.note: "Check back in a week or two" traces to no finding: it is a calendar interval Pip supplies itself (rules 6 and 8). "We" does not match the standing decision that Pip speaks as "I"/"it". The leave-full-pruning-for-now stance rests on AF-3, which is split (C-1). "Dormant" is not tied to a finding about how a gardener can tell. The "still remove wood" sentence needs the same go-gently condition (AF-17) when the rose may already be in leaf.
results.suggested_wording: Since I can't be sure your rose is still dormant, I'll leave full pruning for now. You can still remove wood that is dead, damaged or diseased; if the rose has new leaves, go gently so you do not damage them.

results.note: "Don't shorten or shape healthy canes today" is a flat ban. AF-3 gives a cost for heavy pruning (OSU "any type of heavy pruning ... potential to reduce flowering") and DA-APR says the aim is to remove dead or damaged wood "and give the plant some shape"; AEX-615970 says pruning is fine until a couple of inches of new growth. A ban on all shortening or shaping is more than the finding says and ignores the split (C-1). "Remove only the wood you've confirmed" rests on the Founder photo-limit decision, not a finding: acceptable as framing.
results.suggested_wording: Remove only the wood you are sure is dead, damaged or diseased. Heavy pruning of healthy canes at this stage can reduce flowering.

results.note: Matches AF-17 (Low): OSU-LATE "without damaging the foliage", DA-APR "go a little more gently". Low is allowed because it is a precaution (rule 7), but the record has kind null: it should be marked as a precaution so the Low is not read as a reason to ignore it. "And shoots" is not in either page (they say foliage/leaves).
results.suggested_wording: Go gently and avoid damaging the new leaves.

results.note: "White or pale green" pith: no finding mentions pale green. Pages say "white" (MRS), "white to cream-colored" (VT-BOT), "healthy white pith" (RHS-PG), and AZ1528 gives "until the hole is no longer visible" with no mention of pith. It also departs from the batch 1 answer (cut back to white pith). "Exactly as at any other time" is stronger than AF-19, which only says no located source gives a different growing-season rule (RHS, AZ and ARS pages are partial and none speaks to growing season).
results.suggested_wording: Cut back to healthy wood, where the inside of the cane (the pith) is white, as you would at any other time of year.

results.note: "Cut well below the affected part" matches AF-20 (High; CLE-D, PNW-C, AEX, UNL-L all confirmed). "Bin the prunings" rests on AF-8 ("remove and destroy", Moderate; only two pages confirm it for diseased wood, RHS does not), so High is too high for the sentence as a whole. "Clean your blades" is not in these findings; pass only if it is supported by other research. "The usual care applies" does not stand alone. No timing claim is made, which is right given C-3.
results.suggested_wording: For anything that looks like canker or disease, cut well below the affected part and destroy the prunings.

results.note: Label High, but the diseased-wood exception rests on AF-16 (Moderate), so the lowest level is Moderate. "Sources don't say whether dead wood is exempt" is a research statement, not help for the gardener, and is contradicted by AF-1: CBG ("Dead, diseased, spindly, or crossing branches can be removed at any time"), PTC ("Dead wood can be removed at any time") and RHS-DB ("as soon as it is seen") all cover dead wood. As a gap it also lacks the pointer to local expert help (rule 5). "Sources advise" names sources in the sentence (rule 11). "Exception" is the finding's reading: NYBG says "cut that back at any time, including the fall" and ISU lists diseased canes in its fall section. UCIPM-CB (AF-11, Low) places infected-cane removal in the dry-weather dormant season; the disagreement is not shown (see judgement_view).
results.suggested_wording: Pruning late in the growing season is discouraged, because it can encourage new growth that winter cold may damage. Diseased wood can still be cut out, including in the fall. Dead and damaged wood can also be removed at any time.

finding_corrections.was: Heavy pruning after leaf-out described as having a cost; AEX-615970 quoted as support.
finding_corrections.correction: Split it: OSU-LATE says heavy pruning now may reduce flowering and plant size; DA-APR (commercial) says it might delay flowering a little; AEX-615970 (Maryland extension) says pruning is fine until a couple of inches of new growth, so it does not support a cost. Record this as a disagreement (C-1) with AEX as the dissent, not as a supporter.
finding_corrections.level_now: Moderate (disagreement recorded; Founder to confirm, see judgement_view)
finding_corrections.why: AEX page says pruning is fine now; only OSU and one commercial page state a cost

finding_corrections.was: Many guides place dead/damaged/diseased removal first and major pruning at or near bud break.
finding_corrections.correction: Reword to what the pages show: dead and damaged wood is removed first in the spring session (RHS, UMD, Purdue, ISU); major pruning is placed at or near bud break (TAMU-EP, NYBG-LG, OSU). Drop Illinois, Dunedin and Georgia from the first-step and bud-break lists (they say other things: spring pruning generally, late July, mid Feb to early March). Keep the line that none says whether such wood may be removed later.
finding_corrections.why: most pages support only one half of the finding

finding_corrections.was: Diseased or infected wood removed promptly or at any time: NYBG, AEX, RHS-DB.
finding_corrections.correction: Drop RHS-DB as a source for diseased wood: its sentence is about dead and damaged wood and the page gives no removal advice for diseased wood. Two sources remain (NYBG-FAQ, AEX-236546).
finding_corrections.why: RHS page does not mention diseased wood

finding_corrections.was: Two sources exempt diseased wood; no source says whether dead wood is exempt.
finding_corrections.correction: Reword "exempt" to what the pages say: NYBG-FAQ says diseased growth can be cut back at any time including the fall; ISU-S lists pruning out obviously diseased canes in its fall section. Remove or qualify the last sentence: AF-1 sources (CBG, PTC, RHS-DB) say dead wood can be removed at any time, so the gap claim is overstated.
finding_corrections.why: 'Exempt' is an inference; the gap line conflicts with AF-1

finding_corrections.was: Sources outside the dormant session give the same cut-to-healthy-tissue rule; none gives a different one.
finding_corrections.correction: Reword: sources on removal outside dormancy say cut back to healthy wood, with white pith (MRS, RHS-PG, ARS) or white to cream (VT-BOT); for borers AZ1528 says cut an inch or two at a time until the hole is gone. Remove "none gives a different rule" or mark it as not found: RHS, AZ and ARS pages do not speak of the growing season.
finding_corrections.why: three of five pages support only part; absence claim is not a source statement

B1.judgement_view: Founder judgement is needed on two points. First, C-1: whether the opening should lead with the view that full pruning should wait (OSU, DA, and general guides at bud break) and show the Maryland extension answer (fine until a couple of inches of new growth) as the dissent, or treat the two as evenly split and give both without leading. Second, C-3: whether to show UCIPM-CB's single Low-level advice (remove infected canes in dry weather in the dormant season) next to the higher-level advice to remove diseased wood promptly or at any time. Under the Founder direction of 16 October 2026 it could be left out, since it is Low and one source; the other findings do not need a Founder.
package_notes: Pip's voice: notSureIntro uses "we", while the standing decision has Pip speaking as "I" and referred to as "it".
conditions[1] (go gently) is a precaution and should carry kind=precaution with its Low label.
Several sentences state limits as flat rules (don't shorten or shape, not the time for full pruning); the research on leaf-out is split, so the wording should show that.
lateSeason and conditions[3] labels should be the lowest of the findings used (Moderate), not High.
"Bin" and "clean your blades" are not in the findings given; confirm against other research or use "destroy" as the sources do.
Statements on removing dead wood in a rose already in leaf rest on AF-2 and AF-17 (Low, two sources); keep the go-gently condition with them.

results.note: Question only; no claim.
Framing; adds no claim the research contradicts.

Seven pages say it plainly (e.g. ARS: 'too much shade will not produce many blooms'; UMD, Clemson, Yates NZ/AU, DA, Treloar). RHS only links shade to blind shoots, CSU/Ask Ext/NZRS/Kings only say roses need sun; the sentence does not lean on those.
All 13 pages confirm the figures (4 to 8). 'Sources give' is research talk; and 'Six is the most common figure' is about the research count, not about the plant. The range is shown, which is right.
results.suggested_wording: Roses need at least four to eight hours of direct sun a day. Six is the figure most often given.

results.note: Finding says only YAT-NZ ties competition to light, moisture and nutrients. Other pages (ARS 'Tree roots will steal water and nutrients', ILL, OKS, NMSU) speak of roots/water/food, not light. 'Light' is a one-source claim stated as agreed. 'Sources advise' is research talk.
results.suggested_wording: Tree roots and nearby shrubs compete with a rose for water and food. Plant roses away from them.

results.note: Five pages confirm (UCIPM 'at the expense of flowers', AE-CSU, UMD, Clemson, AE-ILL). Yates AU is partial but not relied on.

Only CSU, Kings and Yates AU were confirmed as saying too little feeding hurts flowering. RHS (feeding as control for blind shoots), NMSU ('Nitrogen is the main nutrient responsible for this required cyclic growth') and RSNSW ('hungry plants') do not state the link. 'Is also given as a reason' is research talk. 'My care tips' refers to app content (other research).
results.suggested_wording: Too little feeding can also mean fewer flowers, and feeding helps. My care tips give the feeding pattern.

results.note: Reduced flowering is confirmed only by Marin Rose Society ('producing small blooms') and Clemson (general: flowers 'dry and drop off'). CSU, UCIPM and NMSU pages do not say drought reduces flowering. 'Pale, limp leaves' is NMSU only, and the page says afternoon heat can cause similar signs, a limit that changes what the gardener does. Dropped leaves rest on Marin and UCIPM (defoliation).
results.suggested_wording: Too little water, or drought, can reduce flowering. A rose short of water may drop leaves and make small flowers. Pale, limp leaves can also come from afternoon heat.

results.note: Confirmed by Ask Ext, UMD ('improper pruning (either too much, too little, or at the wrong time)') and Tui. Illinois page does not say it (supports: no); OSU speaks of weakening, not flowering. 'Is listed as a reason' and 'No source says' are research talk. The gap should point to local help (rule 5).
results.suggested_wording: Pruning too hard, too little or at the wrong time can mean fewer flowers. I couldn't find how much pruning is too much; a local rose society can help.

results.note: Each half rests on one extension page: OSU 'cut the plants more severely' for a few large flowers; UCIPM 'Less pruning ... a greater number of smaller flowers'. UGA does not say it (variety vigour only). Together they give one agreed relation, so Moderate can stand without UGA.
Four pages confirm (UCIPM, ISU, PALM, KINGS).
Five pages confirm (CSU 'late spring or early summer', DA, UVM, GrownUps). Gap and local help follow rule 5; app routes are framing.

Illinois ('all pruning should be delayed until after flowering'), UVM (rambler pruned after blooming) and Ask Ext confirm. DA and Clemson pages do not mention pruning before flowering and are not relied on.
RHS 'develop normally, but fail to develop a terminal flower bud'; Ask Ext, VSRG, Tantau confirm.
RHS 'The cause is unknown', VSRG, Ask Ext confirm; Tantau names the day/night swing. Weather and shade are RHS-linked.

Finding records that the cut point differs (C-4). Sources disagree on where to cut, so the label must be 'Sources disagree', not Moderate. It leads with the RHS, but the three cut points carry the same level and are each on one page, so lead with none. RHS is named though its name is not the point. Each cut point is a single page (RHS; VSRG 'next lower stipule'; Tantau 'next fully formed five-leaf').
results.suggested_wording: Cut a blind shoot back so it can send up a new shoot that flowers later in the season. Sources disagree on where to cut: one cuts back by half to a strong bud, another to the next leaf joint down, another to the next full five-leaflet leaf. (Label: Sources disagree)

results.note: RHS FAQ ('usually caused by cool, wet weather') and RHS Flower balling ('develop normally but do not open'; 'papery') confirm; Treloar confirms only buds that ball with brown petals, not the weather. 'Feels soft' is not among the page words confirmed (inner-petals sentence seen only in paraphrase). Cause and signs rest on the RHS alone.
results.suggested_wording: Buds that form but don't open after cool, wet weather may be 'balled': the outer petals dry into a brown, papery shell.

results.note: RHS confirms 'Remove balled buds promptly before grey mould sets in'. Air flow and no overhead watering are Treloar (botrytis page) only, so 'sources ... suggest' overstates; it is one source. 'Rotting buds' is not on the RHS page.
results.suggested_wording: Remove balled buds promptly, before grey mould sets in. One source also suggests better air flow around the plant and watering at the base, not over the leaves.

results.note: UW/UC Davis ('spotted flower petals ... woolly gray fungal spores') and Treloar ('more prevalent in cool, wet weather') confirm. RHS page is not used for symptoms. 'Sources link' is slightly research-flavoured but harmless.
UCIPM 'streak with brown or become distorted', UMD, UGA, UW confirm.
RSWA ('burrow into buds'), UCIPM ('bore into flower buds'), Yates ('Holes in flower buds') together support holes in buds and caterpillars.

Fewer flowers is stated by OKS-BS ('Repeated severe defoliation weakens the plant so that it produces fewer and poorer quality blooms') and CSU in part. UMD and UAEX say only foliage loss / weakening. The sentence drops the condition 'repeated severe' leaf loss and states it as certain.
results.suggested_wording: Black spot (dark spots on the leaves, then yellowing and leaf drop) can weaken a rose. Repeated severe leaf loss means fewer, poorer flowers.

results.note: Framing only.
RHS-BLIND, Ask Ext, VSRG, Tantau confirm.
RHS 'Leaf and stem growth can appear perfectly healthy'.
The tip look is Tantau ('no longer visible or even dried up'); no other confirmed page gives it, and 'empty' is a paraphrase. A one-page detail carries the High label of the whole finding.
results.suggested_wording: One source says the tip may be missing or dried up.

results.note: Pages say 'The cause is unknown' (RHS) and 'A single proven and accepted cause is still unknown' (VSRG). 'Nobody knows for certain' is wider than that and adds certainty.
results.suggested_wording: The cause of blind shoots isn't known.

results.note: Photo rule, not a finding.
Question only.
Label only.

'Then it isn't a blind shoot' follows from the definition (no terminal bud). 'Leave it to flower' is an instruction and a certainty no finding gives: a shoot with a bud may still fail to open (balling, thrips, budworm in the same answer).
results.suggested_wording: Then it isn't a blind shoot.

results.note: No claim beyond the photo rule.
Question only.

RHS page confirms 'back by half to a strong bud' and 'should produce flowers later in the season'. It is one source, and the next line says sources differ, so this is one side of a disagreement, not Moderate agreed advice.
results.suggested_wording: One source cuts the blind shoot back by about half, to a strong bud. This should give a new shoot that can flower later in the season.

results.note: Says sources differ yet is labelled Moderate; a disagreement is marked 'Sources disagree' in place of a level. Cut points (VSRG 'next lower stipule', Tantau 'next fully formed five-leaf') are each one page; 'leaf joint' is a plain paraphrase of stipule, not confirmed as exact.
results.suggested_wording: Sources disagree on where to cut: one cuts to the next leaf joint down, another to the next full five-leaflet leaf. (Label: Sources disagree)

results.note: VSRG confirms removal of a short blind shoot from old wood low on the plant ('It will never do anything'). It is one page, so Moderate is more than it supports.
results.suggested_wording: One source removes a short blind shoot growing low on old wood completely.

finding_corrections.was: Cites RHS-BLIND, CSU, Ask Ext, NZRS-FAQ, KINGS as support that shade reduces flowering
finding_corrections.correction: Rest on TRE-SH, ARS-RRP, DA-BAS, YAT-NZ, YAT-AU, UMD, CLEM. RHS links shade only to blind shoots; CSU, Ask Ext, NZRS, Kings say roses need sun, not that shade cuts flowers.
finding_corrections.why: Five cited pages confirm only part (7 pages confirm fully).

finding_corrections.was: Competition for light, water and nutrients as agreed
finding_corrections.correction: Roots compete for water and nutrients (ARS, ILL, OKS, NMSU, YAT-NZ). Competition for light is YAT-NZ only; record as one source.
finding_corrections.why: Light is on one page.

finding_corrections.was: Too little feeding as cause, from RHS, NMSU, RSNSW and others
finding_corrections.correction: Cause confirmed by CSU, Kings, Yates AU only. RHS gives feeding as a control for blind shoots; NMSU and RSNSW say feed regularly without linking it to flowering. Drop them as support for the cause.
finding_corrections.why: Three pages partial; three confirm.

finding_corrections.was: Too little water reduces flowering, from CSU, UCIPM, NMSU, Clemson, Marin
finding_corrections.correction: Reduced flowering confirmed by Marin (small blooms) and Clemson (general plants) only. CSU gives a water amount; UCIPM links drought to leaf loss and cane sunburn; NMSU gives pale limp leaves as a sign and says afternoon heat can look similar. Add that limitation.
finding_corrections.why: Three of five pages do not state flowering loss; one source is general, not rose.

finding_corrections.was: Improper pruning as cause, incl. Illinois and OSU
finding_corrections.correction: Confirmed by Ask Ext, UMD, Tui. Drop Illinois (describes how hard to prune, not a cause). OSU says weakening, not poor flowering.
finding_corrections.why: Illinois supports: no; OSU partial.

finding_corrections.was: Harder pruning gives fewer, larger flowers; lighter gives more, smaller (OSU, UCIPM, UGA)
finding_corrections.correction: Drop UGA (variety vigour only). Harder half rests on OSU; lighter half on UCIPM.

finding_corrections.was: Cites DA-FAQ and CLEM as support
finding_corrections.correction: Drop DA-FAQ (flowers on older growth, nothing on pruning) and CLEM (climbers, severe cutting) as support for pruning before flowering removes flowers. Keep ILL-PRUNE, AE-UVM, Ask Ext.
finding_corrections.why: Two pages partial; three confirm.

finding_corrections.was: Cut-back of blind shoots as one Moderate finding with a differing cut point
finding_corrections.correction: Record as a disagreement on where to cut: RHS (half to a strong bud), VSRG (next lower stipule), Tantau (next fully formed five-leaf), each on one page. The cut-back itself is agreed. Short blind shoot on old wood removed entirely is VSRG alone. Under the 16 Oct direction Tantau (a breeder) disagreeing with a recognised body may be left out, VSRG then remains.
finding_corrections.why: Disagreement; each cut on one page.

finding_corrections.was: Balling cause, signs and susceptibility as one Moderate finding
finding_corrections.correction: Buds not opening with brown petals: RHS and Treloar. Cool, wet weather cause, papery shell and softness: RHS pages only (Treloar silent on weather); 'feels soft' not among confirmed words. Record those as one source.
finding_corrections.why: Treloar supports only part; RHS two pages are one source.

finding_corrections.was: Remove buds, improve air flow, avoid overhead water as agreed
finding_corrections.correction: RHS confirms prompt removal of balled buds only. Air flow and no overhead watering are Treloar (botrytis) only. Record C-7 (RHS: no chemical treatments for balling; Treloar fungicide for botrytis).
finding_corrections.why: RHS page lacks Treloar advice.

finding_corrections.was: RHS-BALL cited for botrytis symptoms
finding_corrections.correction: RHS says grey mould can follow balling; it does not describe spotted petals. Symptoms and cool, wet weather rest on UW (UC Davis) and Treloar.
finding_corrections.why: RHS quote is about removing buds.

finding_corrections.was: CSU cited with thrips petal streaking
finding_corrections.correction: CSU only names thrips as a possible cause. Streaking and distortion rest on UCIPM, UMD, UGA, UW.
finding_corrections.why: CSU page partial.

finding_corrections.was: Black spot weakens the rose and it produces fewer flowers
finding_corrections.correction: Fewer flowers is stated by OKS-BS ('repeated severe defoliation') and, in part, CSU (inadequate foliage). UMD and UAEX say foliage loss and weakening only. Add the condition: repeated severe leaf loss.

results.note: Deep and less often: RHS 'a good soak once a week', Iowa 'thorough watering every 7 to 10 days', Missouri soak to 1 foot. But '1-2 inches' is only Cornell ('one to two inches'); Illinois says 'one inch'; RHS gives 5-10 litres per plant; Iowa gives an interval, not inches. Amount rests on two US pages, so High is too strong; sources differ on the measure.
results.suggested_wording: Water deeply and less often, rather than a little and often. In the growing season, roughly 1–2 inches (about 2.5–5 cm) of water a week, counting rain, is a common guide when it's dry. [label Moderate]

results.note: Depth differs: Cornell 'two inch', RHS 'at least 5cm (2in)', Missouri 'Make the mulch 2 to 3 inches deep', Iowa 2 to 4 inches. Rule 3 asks for the range, not 2-3. Keep-clear gap: RHS 4in, Missouri about 6in, so 'a few inches' fits. RHS applies mulch Nov-Feb, not growing season; Illinois supports as written.
results.suggested_wording: Spread organic mulch about 2–4 inches (5–10 cm) deep around the base — bark, well-rotted manure, wood chips or pine needles — kept a few inches clear of the stems.

results.note: Only Illinois and Penn State confirmed in full. UGA Cobb County lists fertilising in September and 'does not say when to stop', and names a brand. Finding says the cutoff varies by source and region; sentence gives one cutoff. 'Stop earlier where winter comes earlier' is not in the finding or the pages shown (added reason). Two full sources supports Moderate, not High.
results.suggested_wording: Start feeding in spring as new growth begins and feed again through summer. Stop by mid-to-late summer so new growth can toughen before winter; the last feeding date varies by region. [label Moderate]

results.note: Illinois and Iowa State confirmed; UGA 'Stop deadheading' (October) is consistent. Stop-time is a range-like 'early-to-mid autumn'.
Maryland, Iowa State and Missouri all confirmed.

One source only (Maryland): 'inspecting leaves, buds, and stems for symptoms'. The returned text 'does not list' yellowing, leaf drop, stunting, twisting or fewer flowers, so the list is unsupported. Single partly-supporting page cannot carry Moderate; it is Low and not a precaution, so Pip does not use it.

Level Low and not a precaution, so Pip may not use it (rules section 3). Page says 'Poor growing conditions, incorrect care, weather extremes, and soggy soil are the major cause of plant decline.' It does not say 'uneven watering' and does not say 'think about these first'. 'These cause most decline' also adds 'most'. Drop.
Sources are one UK (RHS) and mostly US extensions; fits.
No claim.

Cornell confirmed in full; Missouri 'leave as much foliage on the plant as possible. It is usually best not to cut flowers from a new plant'; Fine Gardening (general-interest) 'less food it can make and the less energy it has to get established'. Practice has three sources; 'past year' and the root-energy reason rest on Cornell and Fine Gardening. Label should be Moderate.

'Roughly the first two years' is not on any page shown: Iowa 'Newly planted shrubs particularly benefit from regular water'; RHS regular watering for new roses; Illinois, Missouri and Iowa notes say the two-year point is not stated. Only partly supported, so not High.
results.suggested_wording: Pay closer attention to watering a newly planted rose. [label Moderate]

results.note: No finding given says full pruning waits about three years. 'I'll check this again next time' is a promise of Pip's own and only about the research, not about the plant.
Sources are mostly US plus RHS; fits.

Height differs: Illinois, UNH, Missouri '10 to 12 inches'; UGA 'Mound wood mulch over crowns (12–18 inches) after second hard frost'. Rule 3 needs the range. Timing: Illinois 'a hard killing frost', UGA 'second hard frost', Missouri gives no timing. Graft union is not on the Illinois or Missouri pages; spring removal is not on Illinois or UNH pages. Four of six pages only partly support, so Very High is too strong.
results.suggested_wording: Once the rose has had hard frosts and gone dormant, mound soil, compost or mulch about 10–12 inches (25–30 cm) high around the base, covering the graft union; one source says up to 18 inches (45 cm). Remove the mound in spring once hard frosts have passed. [label High]

results.note: UNH confirmed; Penn State only 'straw wrapped in burlap', no tar paper or wire collar, so the collar rests on one source. 'Sources also describe' names sources; say the thing itself.
results.suggested_wording: In colder or more exposed spots, you can also build a collar of tar paper or wire mesh around the rose and fill it with straw, pine bark or peat moss, or wrap the canes in burlap or evergreen boughs.

results.note: Penn State confirmed in full. Nebraska 'continue to water roses until the ground freezes, even if they are dormant' does not mention 'after the first hard frost'; so that timing rests on one source. Sentence says less than Nebraska (no depth or interval); fine.
Every winter source shown is a US extension (Illinois, Cornell, UGA, Penn State, UNH, Missouri, Nebraska); none is UK.

corrections_adopted.was: Several sources attach conditions (CBG, PRS, SARS, RHS-REN)
corrections_adopted.correction: Record each condition as one source: CBG healthy rose; PRS not cut below the ground line; SARS regrowth after dieback to the stump depends on roots being 'somewhat in tact'. Drop RHS-REN (general shrubs, not the pruning-does-not-kill claim).
corrections_adopted.why: each condition has one page behind it

corrections_adopted.was: One go versus staged renovation (RHS-REN, CBG, UCF, RNRS, LO)
corrections_adopted.correction: Keep; note the RHS-REN rule for choosing is for general shrubs, so 'no rose-specific rule' is the accurate wording. The RHS page supports only its own part.
corrections_adopted.why: RHS partly; general shrubs

corrections_adopted.was: Harm from over-pruning is temporary
corrections_adopted.correction: Reword to 'usually a short-term setback' (DA-SR 'rarely anything more than').
corrections_adopted.why: wording stronger than DA-SR

corrections_adopted.was: Terms defined differently (LO, NYBG, ILL, YAT-AU, SARS)
corrections_adopted.correction: Record explicitly that a third is 'light' (LO, YAT-AU) but 'moderate' (NYBG); Illinois page does not use 'usually'.
corrections_adopted.why: recorded disagreement on one term; wording 'usually' unconfirmed

corrections_adopted.was: Cites RHS-BLIND, CSU, Ask Ext, NZRS-FAQ, KINGS as support that shade reduces flowering
corrections_adopted.correction: Rest on TRE-SH, ARS-RRP, DA-BAS, YAT-NZ, YAT-AU, UMD, CLEM. RHS links shade only to blind shoots; CSU, Ask Ext, NZRS, Kings say roses need sun, not that shade cuts flowers.
corrections_adopted.why: Five cited pages confirm only part (7 pages confirm fully).

corrections_adopted.was: Improper pruning as cause, incl. Illinois and OSU
corrections_adopted.correction: Confirmed by Ask Ext, UMD, Tui. Drop Illinois (describes how hard to prune, not a cause). OSU says weakening, not poor flowering.
corrections_adopted.why: Illinois supports: no; OSU partial.

corrections_adopted.was: Harder pruning gives fewer, larger flowers; lighter gives more, smaller (OSU, UCIPM, UGA)
corrections_adopted.correction: Drop UGA (variety vigour only). Harder half rests on OSU; lighter half on UCIPM.
corrections_adopted.why: UGA does not state it; each half on one page.

corrections_adopted.was: Cites DA-FAQ and CLEM as support
corrections_adopted.correction: Drop DA-FAQ (flowers on older growth, nothing on pruning) and CLEM (climbers, severe cutting) as support for pruning before flowering removes flowers. Keep ILL-PRUNE, AE-UVM, Ask Ext.
corrections_adopted.why: Two pages partial; three confirm.

corrections_adopted.was: Cut-back of blind shoots as one Moderate finding with a differing cut point
corrections_adopted.correction: Record as a disagreement on where to cut: RHS (half to a strong bud), VSRG (next lower stipule), Tantau (next fully formed five-leaf), each on one page. The cut-back itself is agreed. Short blind shoot on old wood removed entirely is VSRG alone. Tantau (a breeder) is not shown: a single company that disagrees with a recognised body (a Founder direction, 8 October 2026). The disagreement shown is RHS against the public rose garden.
corrections_adopted.why: Disagreement; each cut on one page.

corrections_adopted.was: Balling cause, signs and susceptibility as one Moderate finding
corrections_adopted.correction: Buds not opening with brown petals: RHS and Treloar. Cool, wet weather cause, papery shell and softness: RHS pages only (Treloar silent on weather); 'feels soft' not among confirmed words. Record those as one source.
corrections_adopted.why: Treloar supports only part; RHS two pages are one source.

corrections_adopted.was: Remove buds, improve air flow, avoid overhead water as agreed
corrections_adopted.correction: RHS confirms prompt removal of balled buds only. Air flow and no overhead watering are Treloar (botrytis) only. Record C-7 (RHS: no chemical treatments for balling; Treloar fungicide for botrytis).
corrections_adopted.why: RHS page lacks Treloar advice.

corrections_adopted.was: RHS-BALL cited for botrytis symptoms
corrections_adopted.correction: RHS says grey mould can follow balling; it does not describe spotted petals. Symptoms and cool, wet weather rest on UW (UC Davis) and Treloar.
corrections_adopted.why: RHS quote is about removing buds.

corrections_adopted.was: CSU cited with thrips petal streaking
corrections_adopted.correction: CSU only names thrips as a possible cause. Streaking and distortion rest on UCIPM, UMD, UGA, UW.
corrections_adopted.why: CSU page partial.

corrections_adopted.was: Competition for light, water and nutrients as agreed
corrections_adopted.correction: Roots compete for water and nutrients (ARS, ILL, OKS, NMSU, YAT-NZ). Competition for light is YAT-NZ only; record as one source.
corrections_adopted.why: Light is on one page.

corrections_adopted.was: Black spot weakens the rose and it produces fewer flowers
corrections_adopted.correction: Fewer flowers is stated by OKS-BS ('repeated severe defoliation') and, in part, CSU (inadequate foliage). UMD and UAEX say foliage loss and weakening only. Add the condition: repeated severe leaf loss.
corrections_adopted.why: Flowering link on one page plus one partial.

corrections_adopted.was: Too little feeding as cause, from RHS, NMSU, RSNSW and others
corrections_adopted.correction: Cause confirmed by CSU, Kings, Yates AU only. RHS gives feeding as a control for blind shoots; NMSU and RSNSW say feed regularly without linking it to flowering. Drop them as support for the cause.
corrections_adopted.why: Three pages partial; three confirm.

corrections_adopted.was: Too little water reduces flowering, from CSU, UCIPM, NMSU, Clemson, Marin
corrections_adopted.correction: Reduced flowering confirmed by Marin (small blooms) and Clemson (general plants) only. CSU gives a water amount; UCIPM links drought to leaf loss and cane sunburn; NMSU gives pale limp leaves as a sign and says afternoon heat can look similar. Add that limitation.
corrections_adopted.why: Three of five pages do not state flowering loss; one source is general, not rose.

corrections_adopted.was: Two sources exempt diseased wood; no source says whether dead wood is exempt.
corrections_adopted.correction: Reword "exempt" to what the pages say: NYBG-FAQ says diseased growth can be cut back at any time including the fall; ISU-S lists pruning out obviously diseased canes in its fall section. Remove or qualify the last sentence: AF-1 sources (CBG, PTC, RHS-DB) say dead wood can be removed at any time, so the gap claim is overstated.
corrections_adopted.why: 'Exempt' is an inference; the gap line conflicts with AF-1

corrections_adopted.was: Sources outside the dormant session give the same cut-to-healthy-tissue rule; none gives a different one.
corrections_adopted.correction: Reword: sources on removal outside dormancy say cut back to healthy wood, with white pith (MRS, RHS-PG, ARS) or white to cream (VT-BOT); for borers AZ1528 says cut an inch or two at a time until the hole is gone. Remove "none gives a different rule" or mark it as not found: RHS, AZ and ARS pages do not speak of the growing season.
corrections_adopted.why: three of five pages support only part; absence claim is not a source statement

corrections_adopted.was: Heavy pruning after leaf-out described as having a cost; AEX-615970 quoted as support.
corrections_adopted.correction: Split it: OSU-LATE says heavy pruning now may reduce flowering and plant size; DA-APR (commercial) says it might delay flowering a little; AEX-615970 (Maryland extension) says pruning is fine until a couple of inches of new growth, so it does not support a cost. Record this as a disagreement (C-1) with AEX as the dissent, not as a supporter.
corrections_adopted.level_now: Moderate (disagreement recorded; Founder to confirm, see judgement_view)
corrections_adopted.why: AEX page says pruning is fine now; only OSU and one commercial page state a cost

corrections_adopted.was: Many guides place dead/damaged/diseased removal first and major pruning at or near bud break.
corrections_adopted.correction: Reword to what the pages show: dead and damaged wood is removed first in the spring session (RHS, UMD, Purdue, ISU); major pruning is placed at or near bud break (TAMU-EP, NYBG-LG, OSU). Drop Illinois, Dunedin and Georgia from the first-step and bud-break lists (they say other things: spring pruning generally, late July, mid Feb to early March). Keep the line that none says whether such wood may be removed later.
corrections_adopted.why: most pages support only one half of the finding

corrections_adopted.was: Diseased or infected wood removed promptly or at any time: NYBG, AEX, RHS-DB.
corrections_adopted.correction: Drop RHS-DB as a source for diseased wood: its sentence is about dead and damaged wood and the page gives no removal advice for diseased wood. Two sources remain (NYBG-FAQ, AEX-236546).
corrections_adopted.why: RHS page does not mention diseased wood

corrections_adopted.was: Sources differ on pruning after leaf-out
corrections_adopted.correction: Shown leading with the better-supported view (full pruning now is likely to reduce or delay flowering: OSU, David Austin, general guides placing major pruning at bud break) and naming the Maryland extension answer (fine until a couple of inches of new growth) as one source.
corrections_adopted.why: Founder direction of 16 October 2026; batch 1 ruling on naming one dissenting source.

corrections_adopted.was: UCIPM: remove infected canes in dry weather in the dormant season (Low)
corrections_adopted.correction: Kept on record and not shown: one source at Low, beside better-supported advice to remove diseased wood promptly or at any time (Founder direction of 16 October 2026).
corrections_adopted.why: Single source, not a precaution.

corrections_adopted.was: Minority half-inch figure with Texas A&M reasoning (bud dies if too close, wood dies back if too far)
corrections_adopted.correction: Sources that give a distance most often say about one-quarter inch (about 6 mm) above the bud. Drop the half-inch figure and the tradeoff reasoning, or restore only after a Texas A&M page confirming them is checked.
corrections_adopted.why: No checked page says half inch or the reasoning

corrections_adopted.was: Slant most often away from the bud
corrections_adopted.correction: Record the dissent in the finding: Ludwig's (square 90 degrees) and Rose Society of South Australia (angle unnecessary) are carried only in C11.
corrections_adopted.why: Dissent affects whether it can be stated flatly

corrections_adopted.was: Pruners to about 3/4 inch; general text 1/2 inch
corrections_adopted.correction: If ever used, show as a range (1/2 to 3/4 inch). Stays Low and unused.
corrections_adopted.why: Two figures; rule 3

corrections_adopted.was: Disinfect between plants or after diseased wood
corrections_adopted.correction: Add limit: no page gives alcohol or wiping except Clemson ('periodically', 70 percent); Texas A&M is for diseased plants, general woody plants. Alcohol strength stays out of Pip.
corrections_adopted.why: Method details are single-source

corrections_adopted.was: Sealing advised by some, contested
corrections_adopted.correction: Keep as Low. Record that UGA says 'Sealing is not crucial' and that the pencil-thickness threshold rests on Clemson (South Carolina, 'may not apply to other areas') only; no page says thinner cuts need no sealing.
corrections_adopted.why: Threshold single-source; 'thinner needs none' unsupported

corrections_adopted.was: Rose sources seal for cane borers; not contradicted by wound-dressing research
corrections_adopted.correction: Where rose sources recommend sealing larger cut ends, the reason given is to keep cane-boring insects out (ARS and Arizona support). Drop CSU PlantTalk (wasps called harmless) and Texas A&M El Paso (reason cut off) as support for the borer reason.
corrections_adopted.why: Two of four rose pages do not confirm the borer reason

corrections_adopted.was: Rose Society of South Australia on cut angle (Not assigned)
corrections_adopted.correction: Named in the cut-angle line as one rose society that says not to worry about the angle; Ludwig's Roses (a nursery) is not shown.
corrections_adopted.why: Rule 2: name who disagrees.

corrections_adopted.was: NZ retailers use 'bush' for patio, shrub-category and groundcover roses
corrections_adopted.correction: Reword to: a New Zealand nursery (Wairere) calls a shrub rose a 'bush'; Tesselaar (AU/NZ) calls its groundcover roses a 'bush'. Drop patio. Drop Yates and Tui as support (they show 'bush' used for a growth-habit group and 'standard and bush', not other types).
corrections_adopted.why: No page supports patio; two of five pages 'no'; others each show one sense

corrections_adopted.was: Sources point to a rose society, rosarian or second opinion
corrections_adopted.correction: Say 'a rose society or an experienced rose grower'. NZ Rose Society page supports the rose society part only.
corrections_adopted.why: One source mentions only a local rose society

corrections_adopted.was: Grandiflora in US and some NZ consumer sources but not in NZ Rose Society list or two NZ nurseries' lists
corrections_adopted.correction: Keep, but drop the Rose Society of NSW (Australian) as support for the NZ-absence part; US pages support the 'appears' half only. State the absence from the NZ Rose Society list and Matthews as the confirmed part.
corrections_adopted.why: Australian list is not an NZ source; Plant Store has no wording

corrections_adopted.was: Kings 'Bush Rose Ht' titles are Hybrid Teas, 'Fl' are Floribunda, in every case checked
corrections_adopted.correction: Record only that Kings titles carry 'Ht'/'Fl'; no checked page states what the letters mean. The mapping came from matching names across other shops, which is an inference. Not available to Pip.
corrections_adopted.level_now: Very Low (kept on record, not used)
corrections_adopted.why: All seven pages 'supports: no'

corrections_adopted.was: Palmers uses Ht and Fl in titles; one Ht title is on a rose its page calls a Floribunda
corrections_adopted.correction: Keep as: at Palmers, 'Fordell Ht' is described on its own page as a Floribunda, and 'My Daughter Bush Fl' as Floribunda. Drop the Matthews page as support for Palmers' labelling. Single retailer, so say one source.
corrections_adopted.why: Palmers pages support it; Matthews page says nothing of Palmers; one retailer only
